passage: Uma, when you boss your friends, remember my cousin Pankaj. At ten he ran the lane's games like a tiny general: “You stand there! You bowl now! No, not like that!” The children grew quiet and drifted away, and Pankaj sat alone with the bat, upset. Our aunt told him, “You're good at leading, but ask like a friend.” The next week he said, “How about we take turns bowling? What do you think?” They came back. I asked him later why he'd bossed. He said, “I was scared it would go wrong if I didn't tell everyone what to do.”

qa.q: How old was Pankaj when he ran the lane's games?
qa.a: Ten.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj boss the other children around?
qa.a: He was scared things would go wrong if he did not tell everyone what to do, so his commands came from worry.

qa.q: What did Pankaj change that brought the children back?
qa.a: He swapped commands for an invitation, asking “How about we take turns bowling? What do you think?”

qa.q: How might the other children have felt about the commands?
qa.a: They probably felt ordered about and not listened to, which is why they drifted away.

grounding: A child who commands peers may be leading and anxious, and an adult coaches swapping commands for invitations like how about we.

passage: The rain started just as Mehak's group began building a paper boat contest in the school corridor, and the noise from the roof made everyone shout. “Sonali, hold this! No, that! Cut it here!” Mehak snapped, waving scissors. Sonali flinched and stepped back. Mehak's voice cracked. She had heard her own aunt speak like this before a big meeting. Ms. Uma, walking past, knelt beside them. “Mehak, you have great ideas. Try: How about we cut it here?” Mehak took a breath and repeated it that way. Sonali came forward and took the scissors with a small smile. Mehak's cheeks warmed.

qa.q: What was the noise from?
qa.a: The rain on the roof.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have used such a bossy tone?
qa.a: She may have been copying how an adult speaks under pressure, or felt nervous about the contest and tried to control things.

qa.q: What did Ms. Uma suggest and how did it work?
qa.a: She suggested asking “How about we cut it here?” and Sonali then came forward willingly.

qa.q: How might Sonali have felt when Mehak snapped commands?
qa.a: She flinched and stepped back, so she likely felt uneasy or pushed around.

grounding: A child who commands peers may be copying adult tone under pressure, and an adult coaches swapping commands for invitations.

passage: In the courtyard of their Mumbai building, Gargi was organising a play for the Diwali function. “You! Stand there. No, THERE. Tanay, stop smiling. Everyone, say your lines louder!” Three of the younger kids were already drifting towards the swings. Francis Uncle, who lived on the ground floor and had once directed plays at his college, called her over. “You've got good ideas,” he said. “But you sound exactly like a strict teacher.” Gargi's face fell. “If I don't tell them, it'll be a mess, and the show's on Saturday.” “So you're worried. Try, ‘How about we…?’” Gargi went back. “How about we try the song first?” The kids came back from the swings.

qa.q: When was the show?
qa.a: The show was on Saturday.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling behind all the commands?
qa.a: Gargi was worried the play would be a mess before Saturday, so the bossiness came from anxiety as well as leadership.

qa.q: What did Francis Uncle suggest, and why did it work?
qa.a: He suggested “How about we…?”, which turned commands into invitations, and the kids came back from the swings.

qa.q: What was the rehearsal like for the younger kids?
qa.a: They felt bossed around and drifted off to the swings, not enjoying being ordered about.

grounding: Shows a child's bossy commands coming from leadership and worry, and an adult coaching her to use invitations like how about we.

passage: “Move your piece there. No, THERE! Because I said so!” Aadhya jabbed at the board. Her little cousin pulled his hand back. “You're not the boss of the game.” Vandana looked up from her sewing. “Aadhya, come here a sec.” “What?” “‘Because I said so.’ Where have you heard that?” Aadhya went pink. “You. When I don't want to do homework.” Vandana laughed. “Fair. It doesn't work on you either, does it?” “No.” “So try asking. ‘Do you want to go there? It gets you closer.’” Aadhya went back. “Do you want to move there? It's a shortcut.” Her cousin looked. “Oh. Okay!” They played until dinner.

qa.q: Where had Aadhya heard “Because I said so”?
qa.a: Aadhya had heard it from Vandana, when Aadhya didn't want to do homework.

qa.q: What was Aadhya feeling when Vandana asked where she'd heard it?
qa.a: Aadhya felt embarrassed, going pink, realising she was copying Vandana's tone.

qa.q: What did Vandana coach Aadhya to say instead?
qa.a: She coached her to ask and give a reason, like “Do you want to move there? It's a shortcut,” instead of ordering.

qa.q: How did the little cousin feel about being ordered?
qa.a: He felt bossed and pulled his hand back, saying Aadhya wasn't the boss of the game.

grounding: Shows a child's bossy commands copying an adult's tone, and the adult coaching her to invite instead.

passage: I'm Arnab. When I was made captain of our under-eleven cricket team last year, I thought captains were supposed to shout. “Field there! Bowl faster! Don't drop it!” My dad shouts like that at the TV, and it sounded like leading. By the third match, Abhinav, my best friend, stopped talking to me. After the game he said, “You're not a captain, you're a sergeant.” That stung. That night I thought about the captains I actually liked, and none of them shouted. At the next practice I tried, “How about we move you to slip? You've got quick hands.” Abhinav grinned and went. We won that match by four wickets.

qa.q: By how many wickets did they win the match?
qa.a: They won by four wickets.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel when Abhinav used the word sergeant?
qa.a: Arnab felt stung and hurt, realising the shouting was pushing a best friend away.

qa.q: What did Arnab change, and why did it work?
qa.a: Arnab swapped commands for invitations with a reason, like “How about we move you to slip?”, which made teammates want to follow.

qa.q: What was the season like for Abhinav before the change?
qa.a: Abhinav felt ordered about and upset enough to stop talking to his best friend.

grounding: Shows a child's commands copying an adult's tone, and the child learning to swap them for invitations like how about we.

passage:
Group-work note, Monday, from Tushar (science teacher, Class 5)

Sunaina's group was building the solar-system model today, and within five minutes she was giving orders: "You paint Saturn. No, not like that. Sit there. Give me the glue." Two members went silent, and Aman pushed his chair back.

I noticed Sunaina kept glancing at the clock and whispering, "We'll never finish." It looked less like bossiness and more like worry. I took her aside and suggested swapping orders for invitations: "How about we…?" She tried it straight away: "How about we do the rings together, Aman?" Aman pulled his chair back in. I'll check on the group again on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Sunaina's group building?
qa.a: The solar-system model.

qa.q: What was Sunaina likely feeling behind her orders?
qa.a: Anxious that the group wouldn't finish in time; her glances at the clock suggest the orders came from worry more than a wish to boss people.

qa.q: What did Tushar coach Sunaina to try?
qa.a: Swapping orders for invitations such as "How about we…?", which she used straight away with Aman.

qa.q: How did the group members feel about the orders?
qa.a: They felt pushed aside and upset: two went silent and Aman pushed his chair back.

grounding: It is a teacher's note on a child's bossy commands coming from worry, and coaching her to swap commands for how-about-we invitations.
